e.meaning: name of the chief Norse god, from a root for frenzy or inspiration
e.etymology: From Old Norse Óðinn, from Proto-Germanic Wodanaz, the god also behind the word Wednesday. Odin rules the Norse gods and is tied to wisdom, poetry and war.
namesakes: Odin (chief god of Norse mythology and father of Thor in the Marvel films)

assoc.t: chief god of Norse mythology, father of Thor

e.etymology: The Italian and Spanish form of Vivian, from the Latin saints' names Vivianus and Viviana, probably from vivus, 'alive'.
A recent American name with no settled origin. It follows the sound of Hawaiian names ending in lani ('sky, heaven') such as Leilani and Kailani.
From Spanish esmeralda, 'emerald'. Victor Hugo gave the name to the heroine of The Hunchback of Notre-Dame (1831), which carried it into English.
namesakes: Esmeralda (heroine of The Hunchback of Notre-Dame)

assoc.t: heroine of Disney's The Hunchback of Notre Dame

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Reagan, from the Irish surname Ó Riagáin, 'descendant of Riagán'. The surname became a first name in the US after President Ronald Reagan.

assoc.t: sounds the same as Reagan, as in President Ronald Reagan

e.etymology: A modern American name, a spelling of Alaya with a final h. It belongs to the family of names around Aaliyah and Aliyah that became popular after 2000.
A spelling of Cameron, the Scottish clan surname from Gaelic cam, 'crooked', and sròn, 'nose'.
From Gaelic fionn, 'fair, white'. Scottish poet James Macpherson used it in his Ossian poems of the 1760s, and writer William Sharp spread it through his pen name Fiona Macleod.
namesakes: Princess Fiona (ogre princess of the Shrek films)

assoc.t: Princess Fiona, the ogre princess in Shrek
Fiona the hippo, the Cincinnati Zoo's viral star
hurricane that hit Puerto Rico and Canada in 2022

e.meaning: from the Roman family name Marius, perhaps tied to the god Mars
e.etymology: The Italian and Spanish form of the Roman family name Marius, often linked to Mars, the god of war, or to Latin mas, 'male'.
namesakes: Mario Cuomo (former governor of New York)

assoc.t: Nintendo's mustached plumber from Super Mario Bros.

e.etymology: A respelling of Seven, the English number word used as a given name. R&B singer Sevyn Streeter brought this spelling into view in the 2010s.
From Middle English frankelein, a freeholder: a landowner of free but not noble birth. It became a first name in America partly in honor of Benjamin Franklin.
namesakes: Franklin the Turtle (children's book and TV character)

assoc.t: Benjamin Franklin, Founding Father on the $100 bill
Franklin the Turtle of children's books and TV

e.meaning: Roman name of the River Severn in Britain
e.etymology: The Roman name for the River Severn, from a Celtic root; in legend a princess of that name drowned in it. Milton used it in Comus (1634), and the 1954 film Sabrina made it popular.

assoc.t: Sabrina the Teenage Witch of comics and TV

e.etymology: Of uncertain origin, probably a 20th-century variant of Darrell reshaped with the -iel ending of Daniel and Gabriel. Today it is most popular among Spanish speakers in the Americas.
A spelling of Winter, the English season word used as a given name in recent decades. Wynter is also an old spelling of the surname.
From the Irish surname Ó Catháin, 'descendant of Cathán', a name built on cath, 'battle'. Separately, Kāne is a Hawaiian name meaning 'man' and the name of a chief Hawaiian god.

assoc.t: Citizen Kane, the 1941 Orson Welles film

e.note: Sounds identical to Cain, the Bible's first murderer, and to cane.

e.etymology: The feminine form of Francis, from Old French Franceise and Late Latin Franciscus, 'Frankish' or 'French'. In English the -es spelling marks the girls' name.
namesakes: Frances Perkins (first woman in a US Cabinet)

e.etymology: A modern name without one settled source. In the US it grew up beside Aaliyah-style names; it also matches the Sanskrit word alaya, 'dwelling', the second half of Himalaya.

e.meaning: form of Mary, from Hebrew Miriam, of uncertain meaning
e.etymology: A variant of Maria used since the 19th century, keeping the old English pronunciation muh-RY-uh. Singer Mariah Carey made it popular in the 1990s.
A modern American compound of Grace, from Latin gratia, and Lynn. It is the double-n spelling of Gracelyn.
From the Irish surname Ó Grádaigh, 'descendant of Gráda', a byname meaning 'noble'.
A modern American name in the rhyming family of Aiden and Jayden. It matches Japanese raiden, 'thunder and lightning', familiar from the thunder god Raiden in the Mortal Kombat games.

assoc.t: Raiden, the thunder god in the Mortal Kombat games
Raiden, the cyborg ninja of the Metal Gear games

e.etymology: The Arabic form of Abraham, from Hebrew Avraham, explained in Genesis as 'father of a multitude'. Ibrahim is honored as a prophet in the Quran.
A variant of the Welsh name Gwendolen, from gwen, 'white, fair, blessed', and probably dolen, 'ring'. The -lyn spelling is the usual American form.
The feminine of the Roman family name Aurelius, from Latin aureus, 'golden'. Julius Caesar's mother was named Aurelia.

Coined by Basque writer Sabino Arana as the male form of Ikerne, a Basque rendering of Spanish Visitación, the Visitation of Mary. Goalkeeper Iker Casillas spread it through the Spanish-speaking world.

assoc.t: Iker Casillas, Spanish World Cup-winning goalkeeper

e.etymology: An Italian pet form of Santo, 'saint', made with the diminutive ending -ino.
namesakes: Santino 'Sonny' Corleone (hot-headed eldest son in The Godfather)

e.etymology: A spelling of Brooklyn, the New York City borough named for the Dutch town of Breukelen, from broek, 'marshland'. The double n ties it to Lynn.

assoc.t: sounds the same as Brooklyn, the New York City borough

e.etymology: A variant of Bryn, from the Welsh word bryn, 'hill'. In Wales Bryn is a man's name; in the US Brynn is given mostly to girls.
A name with more than one source: a Spanish surname and place name, and separately a girl's name used in India. In the US it has risen beside sound-alikes such as Amaya and Anya.
From the English occupational surname for someone who tanned hides into leather. It became a first name in the late 20th century.
From Latin silva, 'forest'. Rhea Silvia was the mythical mother of Romulus and Remus, and Shakespeare used Silvia in The Two Gentlemen of Verona.
namesakes: Sylvia Plath (poet and author of The Bell Jar)

e.etymology: A 21st-century American coinage that blends Kash with Ashton.
